strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: FluidGym is the first benchmark that simultaneously provides a standalone (no external CFD solver), fully differentiable, MARL-capable, and 3D-capable suite for RL in active flow control. Table 1 clearly and fairly positions this against DRLinFluids, drlFoam, DRLFluent, Gym-preCICE, and HydroGym.

Strong reproducibility: all environments, datasets (HuggingFace), and trained models are released; the train/val/test protocol uses 10 randomly generated initial conditions per split with consistent RNG seeding; hardware/software configurations and full PPO/SAC hyperparameters are reported in Appendix D; the seeding and evaluation protocol directly addresses the fragmentation the paper criticizes.

The evaluation is substantial and methodologically careful where it is performed: ~16,334 GPU hours, five seeds (three for expensive 3D), performance profiles and IQM per Agarwal et al. (2021) with bootstrap confidence intervals, per-step (not cumulative) reward normalization, plus transfer-learning studies (2D->3D cylinder, small->large TCF) and a D-MPC proof of concept that exploits differentiability.

Reasonable physical validation of the underlying simulations: cylinder mean Cd within 3.84% of Rabault et al., airfoil Cl/Cd in line with Wang et al., an RBC grid-refinement study, and TCF opposition control (~20%) and RL (~30%) drag reductions matching Guastoni et al.
Honest, well-articulated limitations section and a thoughtful impact statement that correctly notes the idealized nature of the environments and the energy cost of high-fidelity simulation-based RL.
weaknesses: Environment coverage is overstated relative to what is actually benchmarked. The introduction claims an 'extensive experimental study covering all FluidGym environments,' but Table 7 lists zero GPU hours for RBC2D-WIDE, RBC3D-WIDE, TCFSmall3D-BOTTOM, TCFLarge3D-BOTTOM, and Airfoil3D medium/hard. Thus roughly a third of the 13 environments in Table 2 have no baseline results, which undercuts the central promise of a benchmark. This mismatch between claimed and delivered coverage should be corrected and made explicit.

Statistical robustness is limited. With only 3-5 seeds and wide confidence intervals, several comparative conclusions (e.g., that transferred 2D->3D policies outperform 3D-trained baselines on easy and hard tasks; that 'SAC reliably outperforms PPO across all difficulty levels') are not firmly supported and may reflect noise. The authors acknowledge this, but it weakens the algorithmic claims.

All baselines use default Stable-Baselines3 hyperparameters. While this aids comparability, it means the reported PPO/SAC comparisons may not reflect either algorithm's attainable performance, so conclusions about which algorithm is 'better' for AFC are weak.

The benchmark's numerical correctness depends almost entirely on a single, newly introduced solver (PICT, Franz et al. 2026), whose validation is deferred to that paper. The added validation here is relatively light (e.g., the RBC grid-refinement reporting is confusing: resolutions 96/144/192 give 4.896/4.755/4.786 and the claimed 2.298% deviation is not clearly defined), so independent validation of the environment physics would strengthen confidence.

Presentation inconsistencies and minor errors: the left panel of Figure 4 appears to omit the MA variants that the text discusses; some references have mismatched years (e.g., Alnæs et al. 2024/2015, Bae & Koumoutsakos 2020/2022, Issa, Pandey, etc.); and the D-MPC is only shown in the main text for one environment. CUDA-only execution further limits accessibility (acknowledged).

strengths: Addresses a real and well-documented gap: existing AFC benchmarks depend on external CFD solvers (OpenFOAM, Fluent, FEniCS, m-AIA) and are largely non-differentiable and 2D-only. Table 1 makes the positioning clear, and the combination of standalone, fully differentiable, 3D, and MARL-capable is a genuinely novel resource for the community.

The environment suite is diverse and reasonably validated. The underlying PICT solver is cross-checked against prior work (cylinder mean C_D 3.328 vs 3.205, ~3.84% deviation with a stated boundary-condition cause; RBC grid-refinement study; airfoil C_L/C_D vs Wang et al.; TCF opposition control ~20% drag reduction matching Guastoni et al.), which lends credibility to the environments.

The standardized train/val/test protocol (ten initial domains per split, seeded resets with perturbations) directly targets the reproducibility problems the paper identifies in prior AFC work (single seeds, reused test initial conditions), and is a meaningful methodological contribution.

The experimental effort is substantial (~16k GPU hours), covering all environments, PPO/SAC and multi-agent variants, transfer studies (2D->3D cylinder, small->large TCF), and a differentiable MPC proof-of-concept. All environments, datasets, and trained models are released.

The limitations section is candid and specific (seed count, CUDA-only execution, limited differentiable-control evaluation, default hyperparameters), and the paper does not overstate the idealized nature of the environments in the impact statement.
weaknesses: The central quantitative claims are shallow and partly unsupported. The assertion that 'SAC reliably outperforms PPO across all difficulty levels' (Sec. 4.2) is contradicted by the authors' own Table 8, where SAC yields a negative drag reduction (-4.696%) on CylinderJet3D-hard while PPO is positive. For the MARL variants the paper itself concedes differences 'partially lie within the associated confidence intervals,' so the headline algorithmic conclusions are weak.

The paper's key novelty differentiator—full differentiability—is barely demonstrated: a single D-MPC proof-of-concept on one 2D environment (CylinderJet2D-easy) with no systematic comparison against DPC or differentiable RL, which the authors acknowledge. The claimed value of differentiability is therefore asserted rather than evidenced.

The 'benchmarking' study uses off-the-shelf SB3 default hyperparameters with no tuning and only five (three for 3D) seeds and ten test episodes. The authors acknowledge this limits statistical robustness, which undermines the very algorithm comparison that forms the paper's empirical core; the resulting insights (SAC > PPO) are largely expected and offer limited scientific value.

Presentation and consistency issues: the Figure 4 caption references 'middle'/'right' panels in a confusing way; runtime measurements in Table 7 are non-monotonic across difficulty (e.g., TCF small easy 0.481 s/step vs medium 0.250 s/step), suggesting noisy timing; several appendix tables/figures are under-explained. These make the resource harder to interpret than it should be.

Reproducibility and accessibility are constrained by design: FluidGym requires a CUDA GPU with custom kernels and offers no CPU path, which limits who can actually use and verify the benchmark; the reset/perturbation scheme is described only vaguely, so reproducing the 'standardized' protocol depends on unspecified RNG details.

The underlying solver is not the authors' contribution (PICT, Franz et al. 2026), so the 'first standalone, fully differentiable' framing rests entirely on the benchmark layer; the paper would benefit from tempering the 'first' claims and more clearly separating solver capability from benchmark contribution.

strengths: Provides a genuinely useful and needed resource: a standalone, fully differentiable PyTorch benchmark that integrates the GPU-accelerated PICT solver with standard RL interfaces (Gymnasium, PettingZoo, SB3, TorchRL), removing external CFD-solver dependencies and brittle coupling layers. The comparison in Table 1 supports the claim that no prior benchmark simultaneously offers no-external-solver, full differentiability, MARL, and 3D.

Broad and well-structured environment coverage: 13 environments across four canonical flow classes (cylinder, Rayleigh-Bénard convection, airfoil, turbulent channel flow), three difficulty levels, 2D and 3D, and both SARL and MARL, with unified action/observation/reward definitions and documented physical parameters (Table 4).

Extensive baseline study: PPO/SAC and multi-agent variants, ~16k GPU hours (Table 7), plus transfer-learning studies (2D->3D cylinder in Fig. 7; small->large TCF in Fig. 8) and an opposition-control baseline for TCF. Results are largely consistent with prior literature (SAC > PPO; D-MPC drag reduction in line with Rabault et al. 2019).

Validation of the underlying physics: cylinder drag coefficient within 3.84% of Rabault et al., an RBC grid-refinement study (Table 3), airfoil lift/drag compared to Wang et al., and TCF matched to Franz et al. and Guastoni et al., with deviations reasonably attributed to boundary-condition/domain differences.

Strong reproducibility posture: standardized train/val/test splits with fixed seeds, public code, HuggingFace datasets, and released trained models; evaluation follows Agarwal et al. (IQM, performance profiles, stratified bootstrap CIs).
Honest limitations section that identifies seed count, CUDA-only execution, and the proof-of-concept nature of the differentiable-control demonstration.
weaknesses: The introduction claims an experimental study 'covering all FluidGym environments and difficulty levels,' but this is factually contradicted by Table 7, where several listed environments/variants receive 0 GPU hours (RBC2D-WIDE, TCFSMALL3D-BOTTOM, TCFLARGE3D-BOTTOM, and AIRFOIL3D medium/hard). The contribution is overstated relative to what was actually evaluated.

The flagship differentiator—full differentiability—is only demonstrated with a single proof-of-concept D-MPC on one environment (CylinderJet2D, Fig. 5). No systematic comparison against gradient-based control or differentiable RL is provided, so the central claimed advantage of the benchmark over existing suites is not substantiated.

Statistical robustness is limited: 5 seeds (3 for 3D cylinder/airfoil). Several headline comparisons fall within overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., MA-PPO vs MA-SAC in Fig. 4), so the stated trends (e.g., 'MA-SAC marginally higher') are not strongly supported. This is acknowledged but still constrains the usefulness of the baselines.

Baselines use default SB3 hyperparameters, which the authors acknowledge may not reflect each algorithm's achievable performance; this weakens the value of the reported numbers as a reference point against which future methods can be compared.

Novelty is primarily engineering/integration (combining PICT with RL interfaces) rather than a new method or new understanding; the paper's own framing ('first fully differentiable standalone benchmark') rests on a conjunction-of-properties argument rather than a novel technical advance.

Minor internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: non-monotonic baseflow drag coefficients for the 2D cylinder across difficulty levels (3.328/3.152/3.619) versus the monotonic trend in 3D; reference-list typos ('fuid'), citation-key year mismatches, and a figure title ('FluidGym Score Distributions') that does not match the caption.
CUDA-only execution with no CPU fallback restricts accessibility for users without NVIDIA GPUs, which is a practical barrier for a benchmark whose stated goal is lowering the entry barrier.

strengths: Addresses a real and well-motivated gap: RL for active flow control suffers from fragmented setups, inconsistent evaluation, and poor reproducibility; FluidGym provides a standardized benchmark suite for this area.

The benchmark is technically substantial: a standalone PyTorch stack, no external CFD solver dependency, end-to-end differentiability, SARL/MARL support, and 2D/3D environments with standard interfaces such as Gymnasium, PettingZoo, Stable-Baselines3, and TorchRL.

The environment collection is diverse and relevant, covering cylinder flow, Rayleigh-Bénard convection, airfoil flow, and turbulent channel flow, with multiple difficulty levels, domain-size variants, and transfer-learning studies.

The experimental effort is large and impressive: over 25k GPU hours, 5 seeds, train/val/test splits, performance profiles, IQM aggregation, and baseline comparisons against PPO, SAC, DPC, TD-MPC, PD control, and opposition control.

The paper adopts modern RL evaluation practices, including performance profiles and interquartile means, and releases environments, datasets, and trained models, which could facilitate future comparisons.
The limitations section is honest and covers important issues: limited seeds, CUDA-only execution, DPC evaluated only on a subset, and default hyperparameters rather than optimized baselines.

The qualitative visualizations and per-environment tables provide useful insight into learned control behavior, including emerging coordinated multi-agent actuation patterns in RBC and transfer across domain sizes.

The impact statement is appropriate: it notes potential energy-efficiency benefits while acknowledging risks from deploying learned controllers in safety-critical settings and the computational cost of high-fidelity simulation.
weaknesses: The core novelty is mostly engineering integration of the existing PICT solver into a benchmark suite, rather than a new method or fundamental scientific advance; this is acceptable for a benchmark paper but limits originality.

The baseline evaluation is weak for a benchmark whose goal is algorithm comparison: PPO and SAC use off-the-shelf SB3 hyperparameters, PPO uses [64, 64] networks while SAC uses [256, 256], and PPO is configured on CPU while SAC uses CUDA. Algorithm differences may therefore reflect hyperparameters or implementation details rather than algorithmic quality.

Statistical robustness is limited by only five seeds, and several comparisons lie within confidence intervals. The paper acknowledges this, but it weakens the central empirical claims about algorithm ranking.

The DPC evaluation has serious issues: DPC is run on only two environments, training degraded and was stopped after 10k steps, and the reported learning rate is α = 1 × 10^3 in Appendix D.3, which is almost certainly a typo for 1e-3 and impedes reproducibility.

Claims that DPC achieves 'one and two orders of magnitude' speedups are based on training steps rather than wall-clock time, while the paper later reports DPC requires 1.5–2× higher training time than standard RL. This is confusing and potentially misleading.

The DPC final test performance is often worse than standard RL baselines (e.g., Table 9: DPC 4.335% drag reduction vs. SAC 6.697% and TD-MPC 6.360% on CylinderJet2D-easy), yet the text emphasizes DPC outperforming PPO and SAC. The exact drag-reduction numbers also differ between the main text (~7.2% DPC, ~8% SAC) and the IQM table.

MARL reward specifications are incomplete for several environments. Local/global reward weighting is detailed for the cylinder, but the individual agent reward definitions for RBC, airfoil, and TCF are not clearly specified, making exact reproduction of the MARL tasks difficult.

Observation and action normalization, scaling, and preprocessing are not fully described. These details strongly affect RL performance in high-dimensional flow-control tasks and are important for a benchmark.

Environment validation is partial: the cylinder baseflow deviates ~3.84% from prior work, the airfoil differs from reference values with an attributed domain-size explanation, TCF relies on prior solver validation, and there is no validation of gradient correctness through the differentiable environment. Claims of 'high-fidelity 3D' are not fully substantiated.

Some 3D settings appear under-resolved or physically limited relative to the 'large-scale' and 'high-fidelity' framing, e.g., RBC3D at Ra = 6×10^3 to 10^4 is not strongly turbulent, and TCF at Reτ = 550 with a 128×65×128 grid may not be fully resolved.
The paper claims public resources but the provided manuscript does not include accessible URLs or package versioning details, making it impossible to verify reproducibility or the actual release.

The manuscript contains many reference and citation errors (e.g., mismatched years such as Ansel et al. [2020] cited as 2024, Bénard et al. [2022] for a 1900 work, Todorov et al. [2020] for MuJoCo 2012, duplicated Viquerat references), as well as typos such as 'Drgoña'. This suggests sloppy preparation.

The train/val/test protocol is described only at a high level: ten randomly generated initial domains per split, random perturbations, and random rollout steps. The generation distribution, perturbation magnitudes, and generalization guarantees are not sufficiently detailed.

There is no empirical cross-benchmark comparison with HydroGym, Beacon, or other AFC benchmarks. Table 1 compares features only, so the practical advantages of FluidGym over the closest alternatives are asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses a genuine, clearly motivated gap: no existing AFC benchmark simultaneously provides standalone operation, full differentiability, native MARL, and 3D support (Table 1), and the paper makes a coherent case that fragmentation in AFC evaluation justifies such a resource.

The engineering is substantial and practically valuable: a single PyTorch stack built on the GPU-accelerated PICT solver, pip-installable, with adapters to Gymnasium, PettingZoo, Stable-Baselines3, and TorchRL, plus standardized train/val/test splits and public release of environments, datasets, and trained models.

The underlying physics is validated rather than asserted: cylinder mean drag matches Rabault et al. (3.84% deviation), a RBC grid-refinement study is reported, airfoil coefficients are compared to prior work, and TCF opposition/RL drag reductions (20%/30%) align with Guastoni et al.

The evaluation methodology is rigorous by RL-benchmark standards, following Agarwal et al. (2021) with performance profiles, IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs, multiple seeds, and held-out test episodes, which directly targets the reproducibility problems the paper identifies.

The limitations section is candid about seed counts, CUDA dependence, limited DPC coverage, and default hyperparameters, and the environment diversity (cylinder, RBC, airfoil, TCF; 2D/3D; SARL/MARL) is well documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The headline differentiator over HydroGym—uniform, end-to-end differentiability across all tasks—is barely exercised. DPC is evaluated on only 2 of 13 environments, and on CylinderJet2D it degrades and is stopped at 10^4 steps, so the central novel capability is under-demonstrated rather than convincingly established.

The novelty is largely integration of existing parts (the PICT solver plus an RL interface layer); differentiability, 3D, and MARL each already exist in prior work (e.g., HydroGym's JAX environments, 3D and MARL scenarios). The 'first' claim therefore rests on a narrow combination of features rather than a new method or new understanding.

Baseline fairness is questionable: PPO and SAC are run with default SB3 hyperparameters and mismatched architectures ([64,64] for PPO vs [256,256] for SAC), which confounds the central PPO-vs-SAC conclusion. The network-size ablation is performed only for PPO, so the reported SAC advantage may be a capacity artifact.

The benchmark results are weak and often inconclusive: SAC achieves negative drag reduction on CylinderJet3D-hard (-2.8%), MA-PPO yields ~0.1% reduction on TCFLarge3D-hard, and several hard settings show near-zero or negative improvements. As a baseline study this offers little beyond confirming SAC > PPO and that 2D-to-3D transfer can work.

The runtime table is internally inconsistent and unexplained: RBC3D (221k sensors, 64 actors) is reported at 1.17 s/step while RBC2D is 1.92 s/step, and 3D TCF is far cheaper than 2D airfoil. The effect of cross-GPU parallelism on these numbers is not described, undermining their interpretability.

Statistical robustness is limited (5 seeds, 4 for Airfoil3D-hard) with wide confidence intervals, and the paper's own transfer and multi-agent conclusions are stated as emerging/qualitative trends rather than supported results; the '>25k GPU hours' framing does not compensate for the small number of seeds per comparison.

Minor reproducibility issues: the DPC learning rate is listed as 1·10^3 (almost certainly a typo for 1e-3), and several listed environments/variants (e.g., *_bottom, *-wide, Airfoil3D medium/hard) are omitted from the main evaluation, so the benchmark's coverage is narrower than the abstract implies.

strengths: The core contribution is genuine and useful: FluidGym is, to my knowledge, the first AFC benchmark that is simultaneously standalone (no external CFD solver), fully differentiable end-to-end, multi-agent capable, and includes 3D environments. Table 1 makes the gap relative to DRLinFluids, drlFoam, DRLFluent, Gym-preCICE, Beacon, and HydroGym clear and defensible.

The environment suite is broad and well-motivated, spanning cylinder (rotation/jets), Rayleigh-Bénard convection, airfoil, and turbulent channel flow, each with three difficulty levels, 2D/3D variants, and SARL/MARL support. The interface design (single PyTorch stack, Gymnasium/PettingZoo/SB3/TorchRL compatibility) is a real accessibility improvement over coupling layers.

Physics validation is provided against prior work (cylinder mean drag within ~3.84% of Rabault et al.; RBC grid-refinement study; airfoil lift/drag comparison; TCF opposition-control drag reduction consistent with Guastoni et al.), which lends credibility to the simulated environments.

The experimental study is substantial (~27k GPU hours per Table 8), uses 5 seeds and 10 test episodes, and adopts rigorous evaluation practice (Agarwal et al. performance profiles, IQM, stratified bootstrap CIs), addressing a documented weakness in the AFC literature.

Reproducibility is well handled: environments, datasets, and trained models are released, hyperparameters (PPO/SAC/TD-MPC/DPC) are tabulated, hardware/software configurations are specified, and initial-domain train/val/test splits are standardized.

The transfer-learning experiments (2D->3D cylinder; small->large TCF) add practical value and support the claim that spatially invariant MARL policies can be learned in cheaper domains and generalized.
The limitations section is honest and specific (limited seeds, CUDA requirement, DPC restricted to a subset, default hyperparameters), and the impact statement is appropriate.
weaknesses: Several headline empirical claims are not strongly supported by the statistics. The statement that 'SAC reliably outperforms PPO across all difficulty levels' is contradicted in places by overlapping confidence intervals in Figure 4, and the paper itself notes some differences 'partially lie within the corresponding confidence intervals.' With only 5 seeds, the algorithmic rankings are suggestive rather than conclusive.

The DPC sample-efficiency claim ('outperforming PPO and SAC by approximately one and two orders of magnitude') is somewhat overstated. DPC training degraded and was stopped after 10^4 steps, the comparison is in training steps rather than wall-clock time (and DPC incurs 1.5-2x higher wall-clock per step), and DPC's final test performance is clearly below SAC/TD-MPC on several tasks (e.g., CylinderJet2D-medium ~10% vs ~21%).

There are text/table inconsistencies. Section 4.3 reports ~8% drag reduction for SAC and ~7.2% for DPC on CylinderJet2D-easy, while Table 9 reports 6.7% and 4.3% respectively. These may stem from single-episode vs IQM aggregation, but the discrepancy is not explained and is confusing.

The claim of covering '13 FluidGym environments' overstates evaluated coverage: several variants (RBC2D-wide, RBC3D-wide, TCF*-bottom) have 0 GPU hours in Table 8 and are explicitly noted as not evaluated separately. The breadth of the actual baseline study is narrower than the framing suggests.

TD-MPC and DPC are evaluated on only a small subset of environments, so the conclusions drawn about model-based and gradient-based methods are correspondingly limited and do not generalize across the benchmark.

Using default off-the-shelf hyperparameters (as the authors acknowledge) may understate the achievable performance of PPO/SAC, weakening the strength of the algorithmic comparisons that are one of the paper's stated contributions.

Minor presentation/reference issues: incorrect/mismatched reference entries (e.g., Todorov et al. listed as 2020 for the 2012 MuJoCo paper; duplicated Viquerat et al. entries with differing years; 'Sutton [2020] and Barto' formatting), and some cluttered figures, which detract slightly from polish.
